analysis.one_liner: Treats US companies that reincorporate abroad to dodge taxes as American companies for tax purposes.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 12 Democratic senators and no Republicans, never got a hearing, markup, or vote in the Senate Finance Committee before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite tax rules so that a US company that merges with a foreign company to reincorporate in a lower-tax country still counts as American for tax purposes. It would apply whenever the American owners end up holding more than half the combined company, or whenever the company's top management stays in the United States while it keeps significant business activity here — at least a quarter of its employees, payroll, assets, or income. It would cover deals back to May 2014, but it never received any committee action.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary US taxpayers, who would shoulder less of the federal tax burden if corporations that move their paper headquarters overseas still paid US taxes. US companies that stay put would also benefit from a more level playing field against rivals that lower their tax bills by reincorporating abroad.
analysis.who_benefits_short: US taxpayers and companies that stay put

how_it_helps.text: It lowers the bar for treating an inverted company as American: a merged company counts as a US taxpayer if former shareholders of the American company hold more than 50% of its stock, instead of the 80% threshold in existing law.

It adds a second test: even below the ownership threshold, a company is taxed as American if its management and control stay primarily in the United States and it keeps significant domestic business activity — at least 25% of its employees, payroll, assets, or income in the US.
It applies to inversion deals completed after May 8, 2014, including transactions that already happened, so companies could not simply lock in past deals.

The effect for individuals is that the corporate profits of inverted companies would stay in the US tax base rather than moving to lower-tax countries, limiting the shift of the tax load onto other taxpayers.

analysis.who_pays: US multinational corporations that invert — or are considering it — and their shareholders, who would owe US taxes on income they had planned to book through a foreign parent. Companies that genuinely relocate substantial operations abroad would still escape, but the paper-only inversion route would close.
analysis.who_pays_short: Corporations inverting on paper, and their shareholders

drawbacks.text: The bill applies retroactively to deals completed after May 8, 2014, changing the tax treatment of transactions companies had already carried out under the rules then in force.

The management-and-control test only catches companies whose executives stay in the US, so a company determined to escape could move its actual headquarters and senior leadership abroad — potentially taking real jobs and decision-making with it.

The bill leaves an exception for companies with substantial business activities in their new home country, so inversions backed by genuine foreign operations would still avoid US taxation; it targets the paper-only versions rather than the underlying incentive to book profits offshore.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core design is straightforward and targeted: it catches the paper-only inversions where the same owners, the same management, and most of the business stay in America while the mailing address moves to a tax haven. The honest costs are the retroactivity, which changes tax treatment after the fact, and the risk of pushing some companies to move real operations and executives offshore rather than just their legal address. It addresses the symptom — inversions — without touching the broader international tax rules that create the incentive in the first place.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Finance Committee from the day it was introduced until the 115th Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Senator Dick Durbin introduced the bill on July 26, 2017, with ten Democratic colleagues originally signed on, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee the same day.
The bill picked up 12 Democratic cosponsors in total, but no Republican signed on.
The Finance Committee took no further action — the action history shows nothing after the referral — and the bill died there when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US multinational corporations that had already inverted or were weighing it kept their lower foreign tax treatment, and their shareholders avoided the higher US tax bills the bill would have imposed; the shifted tax burden continued to fall on other taxpayers.

for.name: Dick Durbin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill in the Senate.

for.name: 12 of 46 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sherrod Brown, Elizabeth Warren, Sheldon Whitehouse, and Tammy Duckworth.

against.name: Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired referred the bill and then took no action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, markup, or vote.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator sponsored or cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists, but the visible support was entirely one party.

industries.note: Companies that lower their US tax bills by merging with a foreign firm and reincorporating abroad — a move common in pharmaceuticals, medical devices, and other sectors — would have been taxed as American again if their US owners still held a majority or their management stayed in the US. Their gain from inverting comes largely at the expense of other taxpayers, so their interest runs against the public's here.

industries.industry: Tax advisory and corporate law firms
industries.note: A large industry of lawyers and accountants structures and profits from inversion deals and cross-border tax avoidance; narrowing the rules would shrink that market. The cost falls on corporate clients' fees, but the deals themselves shift tax onto the public.

Companies that keep their headquarters and tax base in the United States compete against rivals that cut their tax bills by inverting. Closing the loophole levels the field and slightly reduces the share of federal taxes borne by firms and individuals that stay.
